item.title: What Is PHP? Why Are Government and Business Websites Going Offline?
item.description:
Governments and companies around the world are racing to patch their websites — or taking them offline until they can be fixed — after the discovery of major security flaws in PHP, a piece of software that underpins much of the internet.

OpenAI, whose artificial intelligence models were used to find the bugs, said in a blog post that it was “one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory” given PHP’s widespread use.

PHP, short for PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor, is a decades-old, open-source programming language that is used to build and run web applications. By some estimates, about 70 percent of all websites and web applications use the software.

Services in which PHP is a core ingredient include content management systems like WordPress and Drupal, which help people run websites. Because PHP is a sort of foundational code baked into so many platforms — think of it as invisible digital infrastructure — many businesses may not even realize they rely on PHP.

Security researchers discovered issues in the programming language that could be exploited by an outside attacker.

The bug, which has been hidden in the software for years, was identified by researchers at Calif, a small, U.S.-based cybersecurity company, using OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol model. Researchers from Wiz, an Israeli-American security firm owned by Google, also independently reported the vulnerabilities.

The flaw is the latest to be discovered using advanced A.I. tools, which cybersecurity experts have warned are dangerously effective at finding bugs and weaponizing them. In its blog post, OpenAI said that the discovery of the PHP vulnerability highlighted “how A.I. can uncover security flaws with internet-scale impact, but the same capabilities can also help attackers rapidly develop offensive tools and exploits.”

The company added that, as far as it was aware, “frontier A.I. found these vulnerabilities before attackers did.”

Given that PHP powers much of the web, security professionals are concerned that hackers could move quickly against unpatched systems, manipulating how they operate and stealing the private data they contain. Experts also cautioned that because the technical details are now public, malicious actors can reverse-engineer a patch to rapidly increase their attempts exploit the vulnerability.

That creates an unusually urgent race to update systems. While A.I. models can help spot vulnerabilities, it can also be used to target many victims at once.

The PHP disclosure was further complicated by a leak before the patch. On Tuesday, details of the bugs were mentioned in a post on a hacker forum, which prompted the nonprofit foundation that oversees the software to release a fix a day earlier than planned.

The defenders and hackers began racing to protect or compromise systems on Wednesday when the patch was released. But there were signs of an earlier leak from the group of security researchers working to create the fix.

Late Wednesday, Amazon revealed in a blog post that it had data showing that an unknown actor had used the PHP attack four days before the patch’s release against a honeypot network, or a decoy system, that the company maintains. (A honeypot network tries to catch cybercriminals in the act of doing something nefarious.)

The identity of the attacker was unknown, but the early activity suggested that hackers could have been readying attacks for days before a fix was released.

“It remains unclear how the actor acquired exploit information prior to disclosure,” C.J. Moses, the chief information security officer at Amazon, said in the blog post.

Sites that rely on PHP are vulnerable, which means a good chunk of the internet.

Matthew Prince, the chief executive of CloudFlare, which helps websites secure and manage internet traffic, said in a social media post on Wednesday that the company “saw thousands of attempts to exploit” the flaw in the hours before it was publicly announced.

“That jumped to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes post announcement, hundreds of thousands within 2 hours, and millions now,” Mr. Prince added.

Several government websites in Europe and Asia went offline as a precautionary measure.

The Dutch cybersecurity agency, Internet Archive and the operator of Wikipedia took down a number of its systems. In Britain, the prime minister’s office said some government services might be offline on Friday.

On Thursday morning, the website of Finland’s government displayed a message to users: “The websites of the government are fully or partially unavailable. We are currently resolving the issue. Please try again in a moment.”

Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi of Japan urged operators whose sites rely on PHP to apply the patch as soon as possible. For those unable to do so immediately, she wrote on social media, temporarily suspending websites and similar measures could be effective in reducing risk.

Because PHP is so pervasive, the collateral damage could fall on everyday users whose personal data and essential online services depend on sites staying secure. Consumers could experience online disruptions in the coming days with certain businesses or government services.

Aaron Krolik contributed reporting.

item.title: Ebola Outbreak in Africa Reaches Widest Expansion Ever
item.description:
The Ebola epidemic that began in the Democratic Republic of Congo earlier this year has achieved a grim new milestone, turning up in a third region of the African continent, the widest footprint of any Ebola outbreak to date.

This week, health officials identified a new case in Abuja, Nigeria, more than 2,000 miles west of the outbreak’s epicenter in Central Africa. The news came the same day as the announcement of a ninth case of Ebola in the East African country of Kenya.

Dr. Jean Kaseya, director general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, said in an interview on Wednesday that he was calling for a meeting of all African health ministers on Oct. 28. If they cannot come up with ways to stamp out the outbreak, he said, “the whole continent can be affected.”

Since the first case was identified in May, Congo has recorded more than 9,700 confirmed cases and more than 4,600 deaths, making the outbreak the fastest growing Ebola epidemic ever. Within Congo, the disease has spread to eight provinces, and about 70 percent of new cases occur in the community, suggesting widespread undetected transmission.

Clinical trials of vaccines against Bundibugyo, the type of Ebola in this outbreak, are underway, but the shots are not expected to be available for many more months. And they leave out children under 5, who account for nearly one in four cases and one in three deaths.

Nigeria is Africa’s most populous country, and Abuja, its capital, is a hub for global travel, with thousands of international passengers each month.

The patient in Nigeria had recently returned from a trip to Uganda, raising questions about whether that country, too, has active cases again. Uganda confirmed 20 cases and two deaths earlier this year, but the World Health Organization declared in August that Uganda’s outbreak had ended.

Regardless of its origin, “I see the Nigeria case as a reflection of how uncontrolled the growth has become,” said Dr. Nahid Bhadelia, the director of Boston University’s Center on Emerging Infectious Diseases.

Dr. Bhadelia said she was more worried about Ebola spreading undetected in African countries that may share borders with affected countries than about it moving to other continents. “I worry about South Sudan every day,” she said.

Some public health experts were alarmed by a lack of clarity about the Nigerian case. The patient is a Ugandan national who lives with her husband, a Swiss diplomat, in Abuja.

The Ugandan health ministry has said the woman traveled to Congo on business and passed through Uganda on her way back home to Nigeria. “Travel through Uganda does not establish that infection occurred here,” the ministry said.

But according to Dr. Kaseya, the woman told health officials she did not travel to Congo and had been in Kampala, the Ugandan capital, on a two-week holiday.

“This is what she said, but we need to continue investigation because for sure she got Ebola somewhere,” he said.

Referring to the possibility of ongoing cases in Uganda, he added: “It’s so difficult to comment and to have a conclusion on that if we don’t know the full story from the lady.”

The dates of the patient’s travel are also unclear. The World Health Organization’s Africa office said she developed symptoms on Oct. 7, four days after returning to Abuja. But an official from the Nigeria C.D.C. has said she arrived in Abuja on Oct. 5, two days before symptoms emerged.

She sought care for malaria-like symptoms Oct. 11, but doctors did not suspect Ebola as the cause of her illness for more than a week. She was diagnosed as being infected with Bundibugyo on Oct. 20. During that time, according to Nigerian officials, she came into contact with at least 44 people, including many health care workers, who are now being closely monitored for signs of illness. But that number is likely to grow as officials learn more about her whereabouts before she was diagnosed, experts said.

In Kenya, eight new cases identified so far are all contacts of the first, a Congolese patient who traveled through Uganda before arriving in Nairobi. The patient was diagnosed on Oct. 5 and died the same night.

“One imported case can be contained by quickly tracing contacts,” said Dr. Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, director general of the World Health Organization. “The real danger is sustained spread within communities.”

Nigeria contended with an imported case of Ebola during the 2014 outbreak, but was able to snuff out the resulting cluster of cases within a couple of months, in part by relying on its infrastructure for polio eradication.

Dr. Bhadelia said she was hopeful Nigeria would once again be able to contain Ebola quickly. She said she was more concerned about the lack of information from the Ugandan government on the potential trails of infection left behind by the patients who traveled to Kenya and Nigeria.

“We’re not hearing enough about the contact tracing, or active investigations to look for any chains of transmission that may have resulted around these two cases,” she said.

item.title: Italy Experiences Food and Fuel Shortages After Truckers on Strike Block Roads
item.description:
On Wednesday night in Naples, Italy, a 72-year-old retiree walked into a supermarket to buy himself a snack and found it nearly bare.

It was out of milk, yogurt and eggs. Its shelves of pasta, oils and canned tomatoes were almost empty. The vast produce section was empty save for red onions, chestnuts, two melons and a case of ornamental gourds.

“It’s worse than I expected,” said Giuseppe Crisci, the retiree, who walked out with a bag of biscuits. “And what I expected was exceptional.”

Experiences like Mr. Crisci’s played out repeatedly this week across Naples, a sprawling port city in Italy’s south where residents faced widespread shortages at their gas pumps and grocery stores.

It is the fallout from a week of strikes and road blockades by southern Italian truckers who have slowed traffic on the region’s main highways, making it harder to distribute goods. The truckers are protesting spikes in fuel costs since the start of the war in Iran. The price of gasoline in Italy has risen 27 percent and diesel 32 percent since February, according to government data.

Naples risks “being paralyzed,” wrote Gaetano Manfredi, the city’s mayor, in a statement issued with the mayor of another southern city affected by the truckers’ strikes. The blockades were responsible, he added, for “supermarket shelves growing emptier and emptier.”

The truckers say they have no choice, blaming the government for failing to shield them from the price hikes. “We don’t want to create inconveniences,” said Salvatore Esposito, a trucker who has protested at the city port since Sunday. “But it’s necessary. At the end of the month, with our costs, we can’t live like this; we can’t work like this.”

About 90 percent of gas stations in Campania, the region where Naples is the capital, have run dry, said Gaetano La Rocca, president of a federation representing gas station operators there. In addition to snarling highways, he said, truckers have blocked access to fuel depositories where tankers fill up.

And the situation has been exacerbated by Neapolitans themselves: Fearing long-term shortages, they have stockpiled the limited amounts of food that suppliers have managed to deliver to the city’s grocery stores.

On Thursday afternoon, Italy’s prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, announced that the national government would allocate the equivalent of about $200 million for truckers, farmers, and fishermen affected by high fuel costs.

Since the start of the war in Iran, gas prices have emerged as a major political issue for Ms. Meloni, a right-wing leader who won office in 2022 on a promise to protect working families. Saddled already with huge public debt, her government has spent more than the equivalent of $3 billion this year on ad hoc measures to keep gas prices low.

It was not immediately clear whether her new measures would appease the truckers.

“It’s not enough,” said Mr. Esposito, the protesting trucker.

The blockades, he said, would continue. So, residents feared, would the shortages.

“In the last day or two, it’s become terrible,” said Nunzia Fummo, 53, an administrative assistant who visited a supermarket in western Naples to find it had no milk, eggs, fruit or vegetables. It was also running low on cooking wine, canned beans and tomatoes, and toilet paper.

Ms. Fummo said she was not worried about her pantry supply at home. “But people are going crazy,” she said. “Panicking. And that’s not good.”

Carmela Apetino, 73, sitting in her family-owned pizzeria in Naples’s historic center, said that her yeast and cheese deliveries had started to slow down.

But, she said, she didn’t mind the inconvenience because she understood the truckers’ pent-up frustration. “Someone’s quiet, quiet, and then he can’t be anymore,” she said. “I think it was time for an earthquake.”

At a supermarket in Fuorigrotta, a Neapolitan suburb, store management plastered signs apologizing for “any inconvenience” caused by the logistics strike. The store was out of dairy, meat, frozen vegetables, canned tomatoes and cat litter. On its olive oil shelf, only two miniature bottles remained on display.

“I would drive around looking for vegetables,” said Paola Cosentino, 44, but “I have no gas. I need to get to work tomorrow.”

Very few gas stations were open in Naples on Wednesday. Carmine Ciliberti, a taxi driver, said that he had driven nearly 45 minutes out of the city to find a single open pump.

Ciro Testa, 58 and unemployed, held up a prayer card of a Campanian saint, Pio of Pietrelcina. “I have three-quarters of a tank; I’m praying to Padre Pio,” said Mr. Testa. “I need this resolved soon. But attention: I’m praying that the government folds. Not the truckers.”

Dissatisfaction in Italy’s south is a particular problem for Ms. Meloni, who faces elections next year.

At Gennaro Lubrano’s small family-owned delicatessen, his shelves were still dotted with pasta, eggs and beans. His prices are higher than supermarkets’, Mr. Lubrano said, so clients haven’t rushed his store.

“For now we have enough,” he said. “But we will run out. And when we do, we’ll go protest with the truckers.”

item.title: He Was Reporting on Floods in Australia. Then He Jumped to the Rescue.
item.description:
Will Murray and a camera crew were preparing to go live just north of Brisbane, Australia, on Thursday when they suddenly became part of the story.

Mr. Murray, a reporter with the Australian Broadcasting Corporation, had been sent to cover serious thunderstorms and flooding in Moreton Bay along the country’s east coast, where about nine inches of rain had overwhelmed the area.

They set up in a park along a road that had been completely covered by floodwaters.

“We thought, ‘This is a perfect place to be, it looks quite dramatic for TV news,’” Mr. Murray said in an interview. “That’s what we’re all about.”

But then Mr. Murray spotted a pickup truck coming over a hill, heading straight for the flooded area. The crew had been on the scene for a little while “and we knew how deep it was,” Mr. Murray said. “We thought, ‘Oh no, he’s going to get into trouble really, really quick.’”

Within seconds, the vehicle was flooded and beginning to float. Then it started to sink.

Mr. Murray had already called emergency services for help, but it was clear that the driver was running out of time.

“So I threw off the boots — didn’t quite get to the pants and the shirt,” Mr. Murray recalled. He told his camera operator to stay on the line with emergency services. “I’ll jump in and see if I can get to this fella,” he said.

A bystander, “who walked up much more sensibly in his shorts and no shirt — much more aerodynamic for swimming,” jumped in, too, Mr. Murray said, and the two made it to the truck.

They tried opening the front door and the driver’s door. The bystander, whom the ABC identified as Daniel Hainey, tried to kick in the back window, but nothing would budge. The water was now up to the driver’s shoulders.

“It was a very serious sort of situation, and it was starting to sink further and further,” Mr. Murray said of the truck.

Mr. Murray braced his feet against the truck’s passenger side and managed to pull the door open a crack. A rush of water streaming through the door helped open it further, and “the bloke inside swam out,” Mr. Murray said.

“When it came away, it was such incredible relief because we thought we were going to watch a man drown,” he said.

When all three made it to safety, they embraced. The driver was not identified.

The area had not received so much rain “for a very long time,” Mr. Murray said. The deluge came early in the storm season, putting the region “on high alert,” he added.

The flash floods across the north and east of Australia were caused by widespread, persistent rain and thunderstorms.

On Wednesday, Australia’s Bureau of Meteorology warned that heavy rain and severe thunderstorms could bring flash flooding, predicting rainfall totals of around four inches or more in some areas.

By 10 a.m. local time on Thursday, however, the rainfall totals had far exceeded the forecast. Morayfield, near the scene of the truck rescue, recorded about nine inches of rain in just six hours.

“That is a ton of rain to fall in a six-hour period anywhere in the country,” Angus Hines, a meteorologist at the bureau, said.

“That amount of wet weather will have significant impacts, particularly when it comes to flash flooding,” he added.

The driver told Mr. Murray that he had missed the road closure signs and drove straight through, unaware of the deep water covering the road. He did express regret in losing his truck, a Nissan Navara, which he had just purchased.

“He is one lucky man,” Mr. Murray said.

Mr. Murray shied away from any comparison to Clark Kent, Superman’s secret identity, and said he was just in the right place at the right time.

“I wear the glasses and he’s a journalist, I don’t have the looks,” he said with a laugh. “Two out of three ain’t bad.”

Nazaneen Ghaffar contributed reporting.

item.title: A Cancer Revolution
item.description:
Last week, we learned that Pope Leo XIV was diagnosed with lung cancer. This week, we learned that surgery removed the cancer entirely and he wouldn’t need further treatment.

Not so long ago, a lung cancer diagnosis would have been an automatic death sentence. It’s still deadly. But screening and a revolution in cancer treatments have radically reduced death rates. That’s good news, since rising life expectancies mean that many of us will get some type of cancer at some point in our lives. Worldwide, about one in five people will get cancer. In some rich countries, it is more like one in two.

I had a fascinating conversation with my colleague Nina Agrawal, a health reporter who has been following these breakthroughs closely. We covered a lot of ground, including the tantalizing prospect of a cancer vaccine.

Nina, the pope is recovering from lung cancer surgery. Lung cancer is particularly scary. But it’s a very different diagnosis than it would have been in the past.

Absolutely. There’s been a lot of progress. The mortality rate for lung cancer has fallen and the five-year survival rate — the portion of people who are still alive five years after being diagnosed — has doubled in the United States, from about 15 percent in the late 1990s to around 30 percent now. It’s still not great compared with other types of cancer; lung cancer remains the leading cause of cancer death.

Wow. So what has changed in cancer treatment?

Advances vary by cancer. In lung cancer, for example, a big one is targeted therapy. Many patients have a specific mutation — often in a gene called EGFR — and drugs that target that mutation have improved steadily over the last 20 years. That’s been a real game changer. Targeted therapy, as the name implies, acts specifically on cancer cells and mostly leaves healthy cells alone, whereas traditional chemotherapy is toxic to most cells, including healthy ones.

Breast cancer is another beneficiary of targeted therapy. This is the most common cancer among women; about one in eight American women get it. But survival rates are now much higher. That’s because screening has gotten better, as have treatments: in addition to targeted therapies, there are also new immunotherapies that activate the patient’s immune system to attack the cancer. Those didn’t exist 15 years ago.

Why are we seeing all these breakthroughs now?

Two big things have happened. One is genetic sequencing. Doctors can sequence an individual tumor, find its mutations and then tailor a treatment that specifically targets those mutations. For certain cancers, like some types of breast cancer, it can also tell you whether a patient is likely to benefit from chemotherapy, which can spare a lot of people that toxicity.

The other thing that’s really helped is understanding how the immune system can be harnessed to fight cancer. Researchers have figured out how to better use our own immune system to attack cancer cells. They’ve developed drugs that essentially take the brakes off certain cells in the immune system. Advanced melanoma, for example, used to be almost universally deadly. It’s been totally transformed since this class of immunotherapies was first approved in 2011.

And how widely are these new treatments available?

In the U.S., where a lot of this research happens, the treatments that are approved are generally covered to some degree by insurance. But even insured patients can still face bills that bankrupt them. Then you have the more experimental treatments that are not yet approved and harder to come by.

A new pancreatic cancer drug, for example, which targets a mutation common in many cancers, is now covered in the U.S., though the supply chain is still working itself out. The next generation is available only through clinical trials.

What about elsewhere in the world?

Globally, it varies. Targeted lung cancer therapies are more accessible in high-income Asian countries like Taiwan, but poorer countries bear a higher burden of cancer deaths, partly because of scarce access. The drug companies themselves decide which countries to seek drug approval from, and they often don’t apply in countries where they think they won’t make a lot of money.

You’ve written about some of the unexpected repercussions of people being diagnosed with cancer now living much longer. It’s been mostly good, but also sometimes complicated.

The patients I’ve spoken with are all grateful for the time. Stage 4 breast or lung cancer used to mean a maximum of a few years. Now some people live 10 or 12 years with that diagnosis. But that also makes it very hard to plan.

One woman I talked to was diagnosed with stage 4 lung cancer about six years ago. In her first year, she lived in 12-week increments, until her next scan. It’s very hard to plan your life three months or even six months at a time. Do you spend money or save it? Quit your job and travel?

Nina, will there ever be a cure for cancer?

We are still a long way from that. But researchers do talk about a cure now in a way they didn’t used to — and some cancers are becoming more like chronic diseases. But many advanced cancers still have limited treatments.

One exciting thing many are watching now is personalized cancer vaccines that can help prevent recurrence. We can already vaccinate against infections that cause cancer, like HPV. But now we’ve had the first big trial for a vaccine to prevent cancer recurring in patients with melanoma who had their tumors surgically removed. The full results were announced yesterday. The vaccine trains the immune system to recognize the cancer cell and then attack it. The hope, of course, is that these vaccines can be generalized to other cancers. But we’re not there yet.

France banned some protests in an attempt to avoid a repeat of the riots that rocked the country last weekend. Officials are pressing resale platforms like eBay to remove listings for looted items. Art Basel Paris will be cut short.

A Houthi strike on a major airport in Saudi Arabia near the center of the country’s oil industry killed at least two people. Oil prices jumped on the news, along with attacks on several commercial ships in the Gulf.

The U.S. and Israeli militaries have developed specific plans for renewed strikes against Iran after the Nov. 3 midterm elections, according to U.S. officials and other people briefed on the deliberations.

Researchers used A.I. to find a major online security flaw, forcing governments and companies to shut down many websites for repair.

Almost all of the world’s shallow-water coral reefs are critically endangered, a global group of scientists said.

Protesters in Indonesia demanded action to stop rainforest fires causing a haze that is making people sick.

The Ebola epidemic that began in the Democratic Republic of Congo has reached Nigeria and Kenya — the widest footprint of any Ebola outbreak to date.

The economy is a top concern for voters in the midterm elections. Our chief economic correspondent, Ben Casselman, explains in the video below how that could translate into losses for President Trump’s Republican Party.

A southern cassowary at an Australian zoo laid fluorescent green eggs there for the first time in 34 years.

The most clicked link in your newsletter yesterday was about dark nutrition.

Take a minute to read this short poem by Emily Dickinson. In just 50 words and three stanzas, she works her way through a single, elaborate metaphor about what is and what might be.

The mayor of Taipei, Chiang Wan-an, has declared a “typhoon day off” as Taiwan braces for Typhoon Champi. The decision did not come as a surprise: In Taiwan, typhoons can affect a politician’s re-election chances.

Chiang faces a vote next month, and typhoon days off are popular. If the storm turns out to be weaker, many will go shopping, to the movies or to sing karaoke. Read more about Taipei’s typhoon days.

Postpartum modeling: Barbara Palvin walked the Victoria’s Secret runway six weeks after giving birth, igniting a debate about maternity leave in America.

The war on rats: New York City is using a new gas-powered killing machine in its eternal battle against rodents.

Abracadabra: Harry Houdini, who died 100 years ago next week, is thought to have succumbed to appendicitis. But an alternative theory involves chop suey.

Kalakand is a chewy, milky dessert made by cooking milk and sugar until the milk almost solidifies. This version uses a shortcut to make the no-bake dessert, or mithai, found in South Asian sweet shops.

Where is this riverside town?

Sevnica, Slovenia

Dürnstein, Austria

Qunu, South Africa

Elmina, Ghana

This week we took our children to visit Aberfan, a former coal mining town in Wales. Sixty years ago this week, a black avalanche of coal slurry tore down a hillside into Aberfan’s primary school, killing 116 children and 28 adults.

At the school assembly that day, they had sung “All Things Bright and Beautiful” and were about to start class when it happened. Most of the children who died were between 7 and 10 years old. (My son is 10. I hugged him a lot this week.)

Aberfan is a shared national tragedy in Wales. It’s a term that conjures tears in grown men two generations on.

National tragedies involving the deaths of children resonate especially deeply. Like the 2008 Sichuan earthquake in China, when more than 5,000 children died in collapsed schools. Or the Sewol ferry disaster, which claimed the lives of 250 school children in South Korea in 2014. In the U.S., school shootings have become associated with names like Sandy Hook and Columbine.

These are very different tragedies, but all of them involve a raw sense of futility and injustice. At the inquest in Aberfan, when a child’s cause of death was listed as asphyxia and multiple injuries, one father memorably said: “No, sir. Buried alive by the National Coal Board. That is what I want to see on the record.”

One episode of the Netflix drama “The Crown” focuses on Aberfan (Season 3, Episode 3). It’s very powerful. I rewatched it this week. Here’s a scene from the funeral, but the whole hour is worth it.

I can’t give you a happy song today. But a beautiful one, one that Karl Jenkins composed for the 50th anniversary of the Aberfan disaster. Here is “Lament for the Valley.” Sit with it.

Have a good weekend. — Katrin

item.title: Above Iran’s Capital, a Trump Impersonator Dances in a Jail Cell
item.description:
Mounted above one of Tehran’s busiest squares and affixed to a billboard is a cage designed to look like a jail cell. Inside it is an impersonator of President Trump. He rattles the bars, naps on his cell bed and mimics his famed Y.M.C.A. dance.

He does anything, that is, but look at the images flashing on the electronic billboard behind him, which depict a deadly American attack that struck an Iranian wedding last month.

“Failure to see this scene is a crime,” one of the scrolling images says, as rolls of yellow crime scene tape unfurl across the screen.

The piece of propagandistic performance art is one of the most eccentric in the Islamic republic’s long history of using billboards around the capital, Tehran, as a messaging tool.

Those messages reached new heights of provocation after the United States and Israel attacked Iran in February. Over the summer, for example, a billboard in Tehran’s central Enghelab Square showed an image of Mr. Trump lying in a graffitied coffin.

Mr. Trump has himself been an enthusiastic purveyor of politicized and ominous messaging to Iran. He has posted images on social media, usually generated using artificial intelligence, that mock Iran’s clerical rulers or depict their annihilation by American firepower.

Throughout the war, Iran’s government and its supporters have produced comedic memes and videos online that skewer the U.S. president and his decision to attack Iran.

Lego-styled music videos, mocking Trump administration officials, have frequently gone viral. Analysts said the videos, made by an anonymous group of content creators called “Explosive Media,” often attracted more interest abroad than inside the country.

Yet the Islamic republic’s latest gimmick — using a live actor in mask and wig to mimic Mr. Trump while marking a deadly attack — has grabbed public attention, even among Iranians who often walk right past such imagery on their streets.

Though the population is deeply divided in its feeling toward the regime, especially after a brutal crackdown on nationwide protests in January, there is widespread anger toward the U.S. leader for launching a devastating war on Iran.

International news agencies have published video reports showing the masked actor gesticulating to the crowd as he moves around his cell, which includes a bed, toilet and sink. Over the past few days, many have stopped to film, laugh and honk horns at the spectacle, mounted above an iconic square in one of the capital’s more affluent districts.

Tajrish Square, a bustling transportation hub in Tehran, is beloved among residents for its markets, where vendors sell nuts, fruits, clothing and gold. It is not a typical site for political statements, such as Enghelab Square, which means “Revolution Square” and is often the site of political gatherings and billboards.

The Trump performance, which has lasted into the night, was unveiled on Tuesday by Tehran’s Beautification Organization, affiliated with the city’s municipality, according to Iranian state media.

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the billboard. The installation appears to be part of a recently announced 15-day campaign in the capital intended to draw attention to the attack in the southern Iranian town of Kuhestak last month, in which at least one U.S. bomb hit a large wedding.

Asked about the attack at the time, U.S. Central Command, which coordinates American forces in the region, said that it was aware of Iranian news reports about the strike and that it doesn’t target civilians.

The wedding was struck by a bomb that, according to a weapons expert and a visual analysis by The New York Times, had been released by American forces as they carried out intense attacks in southern Iran.

For years, the Islamic republic struggled to make its anti-American messaging resonate beyond its hard-line base, said Omid Memarian, a senior Iran analyst at the Washington-based research group, DAWN.

“The war has altered that dynamic,” he said, with Iranians suffering days of bombardment and hearing Mr. Trump threaten to send Iran “back to the Stone Age.”

“The propaganda apparatus has gained renewed momentum,” Mr. Memarian said. “The message is that, despite America’s overwhelming military superiority, Iran is neither intimidated nor afraid to confront it.”

item.title: For Taiwan’s Mayors, a ‘Typhoon Day Off’ is a Major Political Test
item.description:
In Taiwan, typhoons are not just tropical storms that cause flooding and damage. They can make or break a mayor’s chance at re-election for reasons one might not expect.

Several times a year between summer and fall, when the subtropical island is hit by cyclones, city and county mayors must decide whether to order a “typhoon day off,” when government offices, schools and most businesses will close.

Taiwan has been bracing for Typhoon Champi, which was at one point a super typhoon and the strongest storm of 2026. On Thursday, the mayor of Taipei, Chiang Wan-an, called a typhoon day off for Friday, and urged residents to be careful. The storm is expected to pass the northeastern part of Taiwan, bringing heavy rain and winds of 141 miles per hour.

The decision did not come as a surprise to many, not least because of the weather forecast. Mr. Chiang faces re-election in late November, and typhoon days are popular with residents, who often spend the day at home. If the storm turns out to be weaker than forecast, many go shopping, to the movies or to sing karaoke. (Mr. Chiang, a member of the Nationalist Party, also called the Kuomintang, is in a close race with Puma Shen, a popular legislator from the governing Democratic Progressive Party.)

Almost all cities and counties across Taiwan’s main island had suspended work and class on Friday.

Because typhoons are such a common part of daily life in Taiwan, decisions like whether or not to call a typhoon day matter to voters. Between 2001 and 2023, Taipei had 40 typhoon days off, an average of almost two days a year, according to The News Lens, a local publication. Other cities like Yilan on the northeastern coast, which is often hit badly by storms, had 45 days off in that period.

According to Austin Wang, an associate professor at the University of Nevada who has studied the electoral politics of typhoon days, the likelihood that a mayor announces closure of work and school increases 31 percent during an election year.

See the likely path and wind arrival times for Champi

Unlike other policies that can take months or years to evaluate, he said, it is clear within a day or two whether an official made the correct call. For instance, if a typhoon day is called and the storm turns out to be severe, the official made the right decision. The fact that the mayor’s office alone determines whether to call a day off also means that the decision is entirely the mayor’s responsibility.

“It is a very easy criteria for people to evaluate whether their incumbent was doing a good job or a bad job,” Mr. Wang said. When it comes to re-election, he said, “people will remember if the mayor made the right or wrong decision.”

Tickets for many high-speed trains leaving Taipei during working hours on Friday were fully or almost fully booked on Thursday. Supermarkets stocked extra supplies of water, produce and instant noodles, a common staple during typhoons.

On social media, residents discussed their plans to spend the four-day weekend binge watching television shows and sleeping. (Monday is a public holiday in Taiwan.) Earlier in the day, residents left comments on Mr. Chiang’s Facebook page, asking him to announce a day off.

Despite the popularity of such days, unnecessarily calling one can come back to haunt a candidate. Business groups often oppose typhoon days off because of the cost to companies, most of which still pay their employees for the day. Taiwan’s stock market also closes for the day if work and school are suspended in Taipei.

In July, when Typhoon Bavi approached Taiwan, Mr. Chiang ordered a day off on a Friday for residents to prepare for the storm’s arrival on the weekend. Commentators and his political rivals accused him of inventing the concept of a “typhoon preparation day” just to pander to voters.

But not calling one quickly enough may be even worse. When Typhoon Mikra passed over central Taiwan in June, the mayors of the city of Hsinchu and the county of Hsinchu, home to Taiwan’s largest semiconductor companies, were criticized for not issuing a typhoon day off. The next day, as the storm arrived, the county mayor, Yang Wenke, issued an apology and announced the suspension of work and school. That storm left two people dead.

Lai Ching-te, the president of Taiwan, has been both praised and derided for his weather-related decisions. In 2012, when Typhoon Tembin approached the southern city of Tainan, Mr. Lai, then that city’s mayor, decided it would be business as usual.

When the storm proved to be light, he earned the nickname “God Lai.”

But the next year, when once again he resisted pressure to declare a day off during another typhoon, the storm caused severe flooding in his city. He issued a public apology.

item.title: Global Rush to Fix Security Flaw Uncovered by A.I. Leaves Sites Offline
item.description:
Users around the world were met with error messages when they tried to use websites on Thursday as governments, broadcasters and companies scrambled to patch a critical flaw that exposed their sites to hackers.

Many websites were taken down as an emergency precaution after security researchers found major flaws in PHP, a widely used programming language. While recent data suggests that its use is waning, about 70 percent of all websites and web applications use PHP, according to some estimates.

Governments, including those of Germany and Kenya, moved quickly to secure official websites. Some websites were back up on Thursday, but others remained offline.

In the Netherlands, the portal that gives citizens access to government services was down Wednesday and into Thursday, as were a crime tip website and the country’s digital ID site, according to Dutch media reports. The Netherlands Cybersecurity Center issued instructions on how to add security updates, even as its own site was unavailable.

Rob Jetten, the Dutch prime minister, said on social media that his cabinet was closely monitoring the vulnerability.

Matthew Prince, the chief executive of Cloudflare, a company that helps websites secure and manage their internet traffic, said that it saw “thousands of attempts to exploit” the flaw in the hours before it was publicly announced.

“That jumped to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes post announcement, hundreds of thousands within 2 hours, and millions now,” Mr. Prince said in an overnight social media post.

Security researchers using OpenAI’s advanced artificial intelligence models found the vulnerability, which could allow hackers to take control of servers, steal private data and deface websites, experts said.

PHP, a decades-old language that was originally short for “personal home page,” is a critical ingredient in popular services like WordPress and Drupal.

The nonprofit PHP Foundation released a patch Wednesday morning, and security experts said that correctly applying it should protect websites from harm. But fast-moving hackers could exploit the flaws if they are not fixed quickly enough.

The scope of PHP’s importance was evident in the diversity of websites that were taken down around the world in the sudden rush to fix the flaw.

In Japan, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi encouraged business to take down their sites, saying on social media that access to her official website had been briefly suspended until updates were installed. In Britain, fans of the reality television show “The Traitors” were met with a cutesy error message with a picture of knitted mice until access was restored. In France, services on the official tax website were not yet fully restored.

item.title: In Serbia’s Election, Identity Politics Looks to Be Winning Again
item.description:
Hunting for ways to rally voters, the media machine of Serbia’s embattled strongman Aleksandar Vucic has been accusing his rivals of smearing a notorious Serb general, who was convicted of genocide and crimes against humanity.

Ratko Mladic, who died in custody in The Hague in August, was the general behind the 1995 Srebrenica massacre in Bosnia. Yet many Serbs remember him as a valiant warrior who defended his people and their identity from attack by Bosnian Muslims seeking their own state.

Denying his crimes has become a note in Mr. Vucic’s campaign pitch, seen by his camp as a surefire way to stoke nationalist sentiment and win votes before the high-stakes general election on Oct. 25.

“Everyone in Serbia plays the same identity card,” said Vladimir Vuletic, a pro-Vucic sociology professor at Belgrade University. Most Serbs, he added, know that Mr. Mladic committed crimes. But Mr. Mladic was buried in Belgrade, Serbia’s capital, in September with military honors anyway.

“This is an identity problem, not a rational problem,” added Professor Vuletic, who noted that ethno-nationalist loyalties often trump reason.

Mr. Vucic has been Serbia’s dominant political figure since 2012, serving as both prime minister and president. He stepped down last month as head of state to lead the election campaign of his Serbian Progressive Party, rebranded for Sunday’s vote as “Aleksandar Vucic — United Serbia.”

If his party wins again, as many analysts expect given the lopsided playing field and wide scope for fraud, he will return as prime minister, his long hold on Serbia strengthened after nearly two years of sometimes huge protests against him led by students.

Student protesters selected their own slate of candidates for the election called “Student List — Students Win.” It includes no students but, according to some opinion polls, is running neck and neck with Mr. Vucic’s party.

Whatever the result, it is already clear that the enduring grip of nationalist identity politics is a powerful political tool.

For example, assailing the opposition as traitors, Informer, a Serbian tabloid that channels Mr. Vucic’s views, recently denounced his election rivals for hoisting a “scandalous banner.” Its message: “Gen. Ratko Mladic is a criminal.” Politika, another pro-Vucic outlet, said that by making such a claim, the opposition was “demonstrating its anti-Serb views.”

Student protesters, eager to avoid being branded unpatriotic, in May issued a “Memorandum on Kosovo and Metohija,” using the Serbian name for territory that, since 2008, has been an independent state. It rhapsodized over “the blood-soaked battlefield” and vowed to never surrender what it described as “not merely territory” but “a component of Serbian national identity.”

Long before Donald J. Trump entered politics promising to put “America first” and Marine Le Pen of France and other right-wing European populists surged on pledges to defend “native-born” citizens against “others,” Serbia and its neighbors put ethno-nationalism at the forefront of politics. They continue to do so.

That has helped lock Serbia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, North Macedonia and Kosovo, four countries that emerged from the wreckage of war in former Yugoslavia, in a decades-old political limbo.

Croatia and Slovenia, two other former parts of Yugoslavia, have also struggled with identity politics turbocharged by 1990s bloodshed but curbed them enough to win admission to the European Union.

Wartime ethnic passions might have faded but, said Vladimir Arsenijevic, a Serbian novelist, “the 1990s are still breathing down all our necks.”

The rank breath of that decade is especially strong in places like Krusevac, Serbia’s capital in the 14th century and a bastion of support for Mr. Vucic in the center of the country. The city was heavily bombed by NATO warplanes in 1999 during the conflict over Kosovo.

A big statue in the center of town honors a revered local hero, Prince Lazar, a Serb leader who died leading a Christian army to confront advancing Ottoman forces in Kosovo in 1389.

“We will never accept that Kosovo is not part of Serbia,” said Milos Nenezic, the general director of Krusevac’s biggest employer, Trayal Corporation, a state-controlled company with more than 1,000 employees. It got its start making explosives and now focuses on car tires.

Thanks to Mr. Vucic, he said, his factory has recovered from a disastrous privatization that had pushed it toward bankruptcy.

With new city streets, a new highway to Belgrade, a new hospital and many other improvements that Mr. Nenezic credits to Mr. Vucic’s policies, Krusevac highlights the twin pillars of what the government hopes is a winning election formula: robust patriotism and economic growth that could reach nearly 4 percent this year.

That is more than double the pace in neighboring Hungary, where the longtime leader Viktor Orban, a close ally of Mr. Vucic’s and fellow nationalist, lost an April election by a wide margin.

Srdjan Gasic, 34, a Krusevac resident who now works in finance, said he left his hometown in 2011 to study in Switzerland because the city felt “like a tomb.” Returning after Mr. Vucic took power, he found Krusevac “completely changed,” its potholed streets repaved and crumbling apartment buildings renovated.

Not everyone is rooting for Mr. Vucic, although openly siding with the student protesters who oppose him comes with heavy risks because of the governing party’s tight grip on the city. Danijel Ivanovic, a physical education teacher, said he lost his job last year at a local high school after joining protest marches. “I was fired because I had a different political view,” he said.

Yet he has no quarrel with Mr. Vucic’s nationalism and said the claims that the protesters “are not real Serbs” and think that Mr. Mladic was a criminal “are just lies” aimed at tricking voters into supporting Mr. Vucic.

The protest movement, a loose alliance of diverse political views with no clear leader, has stirred unease among some Serbs who want their country to make a clear choice in favor of the European Union.

Historically Serbia has deep ties to Russia, linked by a shared Orthodox faith and close economic and diplomatic relations.

Mr. Arsenijevic, the novelist, said he initially had high hopes for the student-led protests when they began in 2024 amid a wave of public anger at the death of 16 people killed by falling concrete at a newly renovated railway station. But, he added, he was aghast when the protesters, too, started embracing nationalist themes and symbols.

Serbia, its halfhearted ambitions to join the European Union stalled and its dream of recovering Kosovo seemingly doomed but still loudly proclaimed, “seems completely lost in time and space,” Mr. Arsenijevic added.

In 2009 he founded a group he still heads called Krokodil, which promotes cultural exchange and reconciliation between former Yugoslav peoples.

He is a frequent target of death threats and in July was badly beaten in Belgrade by young nationalist thugs who accused him of betraying Serb interests. His group’s activities include painting over graffiti that hail Gen. Mladic as a “hero” and President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia as Serbia’s only true friend.

Violent thugs, he added, “are just a fringe” but their view that Serbia has been unfairly victimized and must stand up against foreign pressure over war criminals and Russia “represents just about everyone in society.”

The Student List, the strongest rival to Mr. Vucic’s party in Sunday’s general election, recently announced that it wants to continue the current government’s policy of resisting pressure from the European Union to impose sanctions on Moscow.

Nonetheless the Student List candidates are regularly tarred as traitors working for Croatia and Serbia’s other enemies in the 1990s, said Zoran Gavrilovic, the executive director of Birodi, an independent group that monitors Serbian media.

“Claiming that Mladic is not a criminal and that Kosovo is part of Serbia is a lie, but it wins votes,” Mr. Gavrilovic, a sociologist, said, because of the Vucic camp’s ability to stir up nationalist sentiment through its control of the media.

His data show that Mr. Vucic got 78 percent of the total airtime devoted to politics in September on Serbia’s five television stations that had a national reach. A further 13 percent went to his party.

Student-List candidates got only 6 percent of airtime while European Serbia, the only party openly pushing for entry to the E.U., was given less than 1 percent.

Milan Protic, a historian who was mayor of Belgrade after the fall of Serbia’s wartime leader Slobodan Milosevic in 2000, said “decades of brainwashing” had left many Serbs convinced that “if you say anything” against nationalist narratives “you are a traitor and anti-Serb.”

Most Serbs, he added, “know nothing of their history” because the topic was suppressed under Josip Broz Tito, Yugoslavia’s longtime communist dictator, and then hijacked by opportunist party apparatchiks like Mr. Milosevic when the Yugoslav multiethnic state disintegrated.

“The only thing they know about is the Battle of Kosovo,” Mr. Protic said, referring to the 1389 battle. The 600th anniversary of the battle, a taproot of Serb national identity, was used by Mr. Milosevic to stir up nationalist fervor that put Serbia on the road to war with its neighbors in the 1990s.

Kosovo, Mr. Gavrilovic, the media monitor, said, “is obviously now lost but nobody wants to hear this. They reject reality.”

Alisa Dogramadzievacontributed reporting.

item.title: Top European Rights Prize Goes to I.C.C., a Trump Target
item.description:
The International Criminal Court was awarded a major European human rights prize on Thursday, a show of support for the global body amid the Trump administration’s efforts to thwart its work.

The European Parliament called the court a “crucial actor in the global fight to end impunity” in its statement awarding the Sakharov Prize.

“The European Union is built on respect for multilateralism and international institutions, and this prize recognizes the important work of the court in upholding international law and justice,” Roberta Metsola, the parliament’s president, said.

E.U. lawmakers in Strasbourg, where the prize was announced, greeted the win with a standing ovation.

The Trump administration has in recent years taken steps to dismantle the court, accusing it of violating American sovereignty and of unfairly targeting U.S. allies, particularly Israel.

Early in his second term, Mr. Trump issued an executive order directing agencies to come up with sanctions to impose on the court, saying the I.C.C. undermined the “national security and foreign policy work of the United States government and our allies, including Israel.”

The administration this month said it was imposing financial sanctions on the court, which could constrain its ability to carry out its operations.

The European Parliament did not shy away from the politics in its statement on Thursday, which noted that lawmakers had in 2025 “expressed their deep concern at the growing threats and the various waves of sanctions” imposed on the court, “notably by the U.S.A.”

The court, which was established in 2002 and is based at The Hague in the Netherlands, investigates and prosecutes genocide, war crimes and other serious offenses.

On Thursday, the I.C.C. called the prize “an important recognition of the role of international justice as a cornerstone of lasting peace.”

Named after Soviet dissident Andrei Sakharov, the prize honors individuals or groups who defend human rights and basic freedoms. An award ceremony will take place in December in Strasbourg, France.

Of nearly 200 nations in the world, 125 have signed the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court and are subject to its rulings. The United States never ratified the treaty establishing the institution, and both it and Israel are among those that are not bound by the statute.

item.title: In the Wake of Riots, French Authorities Ban Some Protests
item.description:
The French authorities banned gatherings in some cities on Thursday and over the coming days, in an attempt to avoid a repeat of the riots that rocked the country last weekend.

President Emmanuel Macron of France said on Thursday that the bans were necessary “so that calm prevails, so that we can protect businesses and so that we can also protect public buildings.”

“The general recommendation is that there should be no protests in the coming days,” Mr. Macron announced after emerging from a security council meeting with cabinet ministers and the French intelligence services. He said that some demonstrations planned by unions would be permitted, though the authorities would propose alternative protest routes.

Last weekend, riots spun out of huge and largely peaceful demonstrations in cities across France. During the unrest, nearly 1,000 police officers were injured and more than 3,000 shops were looted or damaged, according to the authorities.

With more than 2,500 people arrested across the country, French courts were expediting trials. Police investigators were still working to identify other suspects.

Still, the large CGT union and student groups were among those urging further demonstrations and another march on Saturday. Many are calling those protests a “second act” to the rallies last weekend, which numbered more than half a million participants. That has prompted the authorities to move to limit further fallout.

Even before Mr. Macron’s declaration, the authorities in places like Paris and Lille imposed temporary bans on public gatherings for Thursday.

The police prefecture in Paris banned gatherings, protests and marches in some parts of the city for 12 hours on Thursday, starting at 8 a.m. The areas designated as off-limits for demonstrations included around many important government buildings, train stations and tourist sites including the Louvre and the Champs-Élysées.

However, an administrative court in Paris overturned a ban on a student march Thursday afternoon, according to its organizers.

“When the government tries to ban protests, tries to repress in every way it can, we need to stand together and show a display of force to guarantee the right to protest,” Coppelia Moureau, a member of a union representing students from universities in the Greater Paris region, told reporters as she left the courthouse on Thursday.

The union is demanding the end of Parcoursup, a state-run website that students must use to apply for higher education programs. Its members later gathered on the city’s left bank and planned to march across the Seine River and to the Place de la Bastille.

It was not clear how that court decision would impact the larger ban on protests in Paris, or if further challenges would be lodged.

Some cities, including Grenoble and Le Mans, have imposed multiday bans on protests. Rouen, Toulon, Nice and Le Havre banned any protests in their city centers on Saturday.

In the Var department of southern France, which includes the city of Toulon, the authorities also implemented other restrictions. They banned people from wearing face coverings and protective clothing, and from buying or selling fireworks from Wednesday night until Monday.

The authorities in Paris have not announced restrictions on demonstrations for Saturday. However, City Hall said it would remove garbage containers, barriers and construction material from the streets by then so that they could not be “used to commit damage” and urged citizens to follow suit, citing “the risk of further violence perpetrated by vandals.”

Art Basel Paris announced it would close two days early — on Friday evening — “in the interest of safeguarding our visitors, exhibitors, partners, staff, and artworks.”

item.title: Putin Nears a Prize: Restoring Ties With the U.S. While Giving Up Nothing
item.description:
Last October, President Trump imposed significant sanctions on Russia’s two largest oil companies, complaining that negotiations with President Vladimir V. Putin over ending the war in Ukraine “just don’t go anywhere.”

A red-carpet welcome for the Russian leader in Alaska had done nothing to bring peace. A planned summit in Budapest had fallen apart. Mr. Trump had started to acknowledge that Mr. Putin might just be playing him, with no intention of making peace. Faint Ukrainian hopes glimmered of a Trump-Putin break.

But the Russian president was playing a longer game.

Now, exactly a year after the oil sanctions, Mr. Putin has never been so close to his goal of normalizing relations with Washington without having to make any compromises on Ukraine.

Over the past week and a half, Mr. Trump has set aside years of U.S. foreign policy by openly embracing Mr. Putin and easing the economic pressure on the Kremlin. At the same time, Mr. Trump has vilified President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine, the putative American ally trying to defend his nation against a Russian invasion.

On Oct. 9, Mr. Trump announced that the United States would buy Russian diesel, asking for no concessions from Mr. Putin in return. The Trump administration went on to pressure Ukraine to stop striking oil refineries — Kyiv’s most powerful lever — and suspended Russia sanctions that Mr. Trump had just signed into law. Mr. Trump declared that “Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine.”

The diesel deal was in part a political calculation by Mr. Trump before the midterm elections, as he tries to lower fuel prices. But that action and others that followed also reflect the president’s long-evident affinity for Mr. Putin, which the Russian leader has assiduously cultivated even while continuing the war and denying Mr. Trump a coveted prize.

Ever since Mr. Trump returned to office, Russia has sought to separate the conflict in Ukraine from potential business agreements and closer diplomatic ties with the United States. The Trump administration held back, even as it slashed aid to Ukraine, largely continuing a Biden administration policy of refraining from economic deals with Russia until Mr. Putin stopped the war.

The White House now says such deals will help Russia see the benefits of peace. The Kremlin said on Wednesday that Mr. Putin, meeting with Mr. Trump’s special envoy, Steve Witkoff, had agreed to talks with Ukraine and the United States next month. But they would involve relatively low-level representatives, and a Russian official played down the Kremlin’s openness to forging a comprehensive agreement now.

Newly emboldened, Moscow is moving to assert itself as a global power equal to the United States and China, promoting a trilateral summit among them in November.

“In my personal view, victory has already been achieved,” the pro-Putin journalist Marina Akhmedova wrote on social media on Wednesday. “It is not just a matter of the 20 to 25 percent of territory we have liberated,” she added, referring Russian-occupied land in Ukraine. “It is also about how the United States now engages with Russia.”

Many analysts call the economic incentives offered by Mr. Trump the wrong solution to a war being waged over political and security questions. Still, during his visit to St. Petersburg, Russia, on Wednesday, Mr. Witkoff said that the diesel deal was “another example of what we can achieve by working together.” Mr. Putin, in turn, suggested a deal on Russian fertilizer.

Other potential agreements are on the horizon. Russia and the United States have discussed the sale of the international assets of the Russian energy giant Lukoil to an investor group that includes the U.S. government, The New York Times reported. The Times also reported that American negotiators have pitched the idea of Europe resuming purchases of large quantities of Russian gas piped through Ukraine.

After the St. Petersburg meeting, Mr. Putin’s economic envoy, Kirill Dmitriev, said that there was “no question” that Russian-U.S. economic cooperation “will strengthen.” He said that Mr. Putin had talked not only about a potential fertilizer deal with Mr. Witkoff, but also about “different projects such as data centers, many projects in energy and energy cooperation.”

Playing to Mr. Trump’s style of personal diplomacy, Mr. Putin has portrayed actions that benefit Russia — like selling diesel to the United States — as favors to the American leader. That includes the release on Wednesday of Stephen James Hubbard, 74, a Michigan teacher whom the State Department called “wrongfully detained” by Russia.

Mr. Trump described the release — which was not part of any prisoner swap — as a sign of Mr. Putin’s high regard for him. Referring to himself in the third person, Mr. Trump wrote on social media that “the United States, out of respect for President Trump, was not required to give anything in return.”

But later on Wednesday, Mr. Trump told reporters that Russia would not have let Mr. Hubbard go if sanctions had remained in place. The stage was also set, analysts said, by the diesel agreement and the potential for other business deals, giving Mr. Putin the sort of diplomatic victory he is craving after Western nations piled sanctions on Russia over its invasion of Ukraine.

“Even this small amount of normalization helped Putin to really deactivate Trump and the U.S. as potential helpers or enablers of Ukraine,” said Alexander Gabuev, director of the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center in Berlin.

The diesel deal bolstered an argument Moscow has made that the Western countries that imposed sanctions on Russia would suffer without cheap Russian energy and other business ties. Mr. Putin has sought to engage with Washington to prove that Russia has too much heft to be ignored, analysts said.

Russia “tried all of last year to establish the idea that you can do stuff bilaterally with the U.S. short of settling the war in Ukraine,” said Hanna Notte, the author of “We Shall Outlast Them,” a book about Russia’s wartime foreign policy.

“It wasn’t just the economic deals,” she added. “They also wanted to talk about the Middle East. They wanted to talk about the Arctic. They wanted to talk about nuclear arms control.”

Russia’s goal, she said, was to advance “this whole idea that you can compartmentalize the relationship with the United States and do stuff together even while you’re still prosecuting the war.”

The Trump administration’s offering of carrots to end the war is likely to fail, Ms. Notte predicted.

Sam Charap, a Russia analyst at the RAND Corporation, and other analysts noted that an irony of Russia’s rapprochement with Washington was that it may no longer be a silver bullet to a settlement of the war on Moscow’s terms.

Europe has taken on a bigger role in providing Kyiv with economic and political support, and relations between Mr. Putin and many European leaders have completely broken down.

“Winning the Americans isn’t the prize it once was,” said Jeremy Shapiro, research director at the European Council on Foreign Relations. “It was the whole game two years ago. Now it’s a much smaller piece.”

The Kremlin is also aware that Mr. Trump could change tack again after the midterms, Mr. Shapiro said. Russian decision makers, he said, see the U.S. president as “very inconsistent” and feel little security about his approach to Russia.

Ivan Nechepurenko contributed reporting from Moscow.

item.title: Strike on Saudi Airport Kills 2 as U.S. Tells Some Diplomats to Leave
item.description:
At least two people were killed in a strike on a major airport in Saudi Arabia on Wednesday evening, as Washington ordered some U.S. diplomatic staff to leave the kingdom following weeks of deadly attacks by the Iran-backed Houthi militia.

The Saudi authorities said in a statement on Thursday morning that a Saudi national and an Indian resident died in the strike on King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, a city in Saudi Arabia’s Eastern Province that is home to the state oil giant Saudi Aramco. Eight other people were wounded, the statement said, adding that airport was operating normally on Thursday.

In a separate incident, two people were killed and two others were wounded on Wednesday when a drone was intercepted over Aramco’s Shaybah oil field, also in the Eastern Province. Falling drone fragments sparked a fire in a contractor’s vehicle, killing a Filipino and a Nepali, the Saudi Energy Ministry said.

The Saudi authorities did not say who they believed had launched the strike on the airport or the drone intercepted over the oil field. There were no immediate claims of responsibility.

The Houthis have been pummeling Saudi Arabia’s aviation and energy infrastructure for weeks, killing at least 22 civilians and roiling energy markets.

The price of oil jumped about 3 percent on Thursday, with the global benchmark topping $112 a barrel, the highest level since mid-May.

Saudi Arabia announced a bombing campaign against the Houthis this month in support of the internationally recognized government of Yemen, which has been at war with the Houthis since 2014. That was when the Houthis, a rebel group from the country’s north, seized the Yemeni capital, Sanaa — which they still hold.

A fragile truce in Yemen unraveled earlier this year, and the country has since tipped back into a civil war that the United Nations says has displaced some 260,000 people since August.

As the fighting has spilled onto Saudi soil, the United States ordered all “non-emergency government employees and their family members” to leave Saudi Arabia, a State Department spokesman, Tommy Pigott, said in social media post on Wednesday night that cited the Houthis’ attacks, mounting civilian casualties and travel disruptions.

Washington had pulled many diplomatic staff out of the Middle East earlier this year after the start of the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran, the Houthis’ main patron. But it started sending some back in late August.

Then in September, the Houthis seized areas of strategic territory on Yemen’s Red Sea coast in a lightning offensive, gaining greater control over a crucial choke point for global trade. In recent weeks, forces affiliated with the Yemeni government and backed by Saudi warplanes have mounted a counteroffensive to retake the territory.

The Red Sea has become an increasingly important route for Saudi oil exports since Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway in the Persian Gulf, after the United States and Israel attacked Iran in late February. The Houthis’ attacks on Saudi oil facilities and tankers traversing the Red Sea have heaped further pressure on energy markets.

Some ships continue to traverse the Strait of Hormuz, despite the risks. In the meantime, regional mediators have been trying to negotiate an end to the U.S. war with Iran and a reopening of the waterway.

The U.S. and Israeli militaries have developed plans for renewed strikes against Iran after next month’s American midterm elections, according to U.S. officials and other people briefed on the deliberations.

President Trump said on Wednesday that Washington was not currently negotiating with Iran and “something one way or the other” will happen “fairly soon.”

Iranian attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz have ramped up in recent weeks. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps said on Thursday that it had struck four tankers in the northern Persian Gulf that it claimed had been illegally transferring oil. It also said that three more vessels had hit mines in the western Strait of Hormuz. Those attacks could not immediately be independently confirmed.

Shuaib Almosawa contributed reporting from Sanaa, Yemen, Saeed Al-Batati from al-Mukalla, Yemen and Sanam Mahoozi from London.
